無料でメモをノート・カンバン・タスク・ダッシュボード・マークダウン・グラフ表示の6つに対応できAI連携・ブラウザ拡張機能・PWA・自動バックアップもできる「Poznote」、オープンソースでセルフホスト可能
仕事や日常生活でメモを取っていると文章の記録・タスクの管理・スケジュールの確認など、情報の種類に応じて複数のアプリを使い分けることがあります。こうした情報を1カ所にまとめ、ノート・カンバン・タスク・ダッシュボード・Markdown・グラフなどの形式で管理できるほか、AI連携・ブラウザ拡張機能・自動バックアップにも対応した無料のオープンソースアプリが「Poznote」です。
Poznote - Self-hosted note-taking
https://poznote.com/
timothepoznanski/poznote: Powerful note-taking without the hassle.
https://github.com/timothepoznanski/poznote
◆デモ
Poznote Demo（ログインIDとパスワードどちらも「poznote」）
https://demo.poznote.com/login.php
◆Poznoteの利用方法
・ノートを作成する
Poznoteを起動後、ブラウザで「http://localhost:8040」にアクセスして画面の「＋」から「Rich text note」で新しいノートを作成し「記事制作のメモ」というタイトルで見出しや本文を入力すると文章が自動保存されます。
記号を使って見出しや箇条書きを記述するMarkdown形式にも対応しています。
Markdownノートではプレビューに加え、Mermaidという記述方式によるフローチャートやLaTeXによる数式も表示できるため、技術資料の整理にも利用できます。
なお、リッチテキスト形式のノートはHTMLファイル、Markdown形式のノートはMarkdownファイルとして保存されるため、ほかのエディターでも利用できます。
・タスクとカンバンで作業を管理
「＋」から「Task List」を選択するとタスクリストが作成できタスクを登録すると、タスクごとに期限や重要度が設定でき全体の進捗状況も確認できます。
サイドメニューの「Tasks」アイコンをクリックすると複数のノートに分散したタスクの一覧が表示され「未完了」「重要」「期限超過」などで絞り込めます。
サイドメニューの「Folders」アイコンをクリックすると作成したフォルダー一覧が表示されるので任意のフォルダーをクリック。
カンバン表示になりサブフォルダーがそれぞれのカラムに切り替わります。ノートはカラム内のカードとして表示されるので「未着手」から「作業中」へドラッグすると…
ノート自体が対応するカラムのフォルダーへ移動し、情報の分類と作業の進行状況を同時に整理できます。
◆さまざまな表示機能
サイドメニューの「Dashboard」アイコンをクリックするとダッシュボード画面となりフォルダーや最近更新したノートなどがまとまって表示され、保存したメモを探す際にはタイトル・本文・タグによる検索も利用できます。
ノート同士にリンクを設定してサイドメニューの「Graph」をクリックするとそれぞれのノートが点で関連付けが線で表示され、複数の情報がどのようにつながっているかを視覚的に確認できます。
「Diary」では「Create today's entry」からその日の日記を作成でき、日付別に整理された記録がカードで表示されます。
◆AIを使ってノートを検索・要約
設定でAI Assistantを有効にしてOpenAI・Claude・Ollamaなどの接続先とモデルを設定すると「AI ASSISTANT」欄を開くことができます。
チャット欄に「記事制作に関するノートを要約してください」と入力すると、AIがノートを検索・参照して回答が返ってきました。
ノートの新規作成も可能で「記事制作の進捗をまとめた新しいノートを作成してください」と指示すると、チェックリストや進捗状況を記載したノートが作成されました。その他、既存のノートの編集やタグ付けが可能です。
◆その他の便利な機能
Chrome拡張機能「Poznote URL Saver」を追加してサーバーと接続すれば、閲覧中のWebページのURLやページ全体のスクリーンショットをノートとして保存できます。拡張機能のアイコンをクリックして「Save URL」を選択すると…
新規ノートとしてWebページのURLが保存されます。
スマートフォンではブラウザからPWAとしてホーム画面に追加して利用でき、Androidではほかのアプリの共有メニューからURLをPoznoteへ送ることもできます。
バックアップは設定画面からZIPで取得できるほか、管理者が保存先と周期を指定して自動実行でき、GitHub・GitLab・Forgejoとの同期やS3互換ストレージへの保存にも対応しています。
PoznoteはWebページなど外部の情報を収集する用途というよりも、自分で記録したメモや資料をノート・タスク・カンバンなどの形式で整理し、必要に応じてAIで検索・活用するためのツールとなっています。
◆Poznoteの構築方法
今回はWindowsにDocker DesktopとGit for WindowsのGit Bashを用意した環境で構築します。作業フォルダーにて以下のコマンドを実行します。
mkdir poznote cd poznote curl -o .env https://raw.githubusercontent.com/timothepoznanski/poznote/main/.env.template curl -o docker-compose.yml https://raw.githubusercontent.com/timothepoznanski/poznote/main/docker-compose.yml
コンテナを起動。
docker compose up -d
ブラウザで「http://localhost:8040」にアクセスするとログイン画面が表示されるので「Username or Email」に「admin_change_me」を入力し「Password」に「admin」を入力して「Login」をクリック。
初期アカウント名およびパスワードは変更する必要があるので「Username」にアカウント名、「New password」「Confirm password」にパスワードを改めて入力して「Start using Poznote」をクリック。
初期ノート画面が表示されれば構築完了です。

ai_industry.title: AI-assisted PCB design for KiCad 10
ai_industry.summary_original: AI-assisted PCB design for KiCAD 10. Native KiCAD plugin — a single Rust binary exposing 217 schematic, layout, routing, placement, design-review, and manufacturing tools to Claude, or the LLM of y...
ai_industry.content_original:
AI-assisted PCB design for KiCAD 10. Konnect is a native KiCAD plugin — a single Rust binary — that lets Claude and other AI assistants design schematics and PCBs through the Model Context Protocol (MCP).
228 tools across 21 on-demand toolsets. Schematic capture, PCB layout and routing, ERC/DRC, design-review audits, JLCPCB part search, reference circuits, and a full manufacturing export pipeline — with bundled skills and agents that teach Claude KiCAD conventions out of the box.
Status: beta. The core toolchain is tested and working, but this is a young release and it wants real-world mileage and review. Issues and PRs are welcome — see CONTRIBUTING.md and the naming conventions.
Nimrod is our web-research MCP server: quality-scored Google search, clean webpage extraction, and deep multi-source research. Design the board with Konnect while Nimrod pulls live parts availability, datasheets, and errata — no more guessing from year-old training data
- Works with claude.ai, Claude Desktop, Claude Code, VS Code, and any MCP client
- 1 credit = 1 search · extraction always free · free 50-credit trial, no card
- Official MCP Registry: ai.orchis/nimrod
Konnect is the successor to KiCAD-MCP-Server, a Python/TypeScript project that proved AI-driven PCB design works — and, in the process, showed exactly where that architecture runs out of road. Konnect was built to fix those specific problems:
The call path was too long. In the original server, a single tool call travels through TypeScript, schema validation, a spawned Python subprocess, JSON over stdin/stdout, a command router, and finally SWIG-generated C++ proxy objects before anything touches your board. That's four language and serialization boundaries, each with its own failure modes — subprocess lifecycle management, stdout parsing that filters out warnings KiCAD leaks into the stream, chunked-JSON reassembly. In Konnect, a tool call is a function call. One process, one language, no plumbing.
The dependency surface was enormous. Running the original means carrying Node.js and its npm tree, Python and its pip packages, wxPython, kicad-skip, and KiCAD's SWIG bindings — two package ecosystems plus a binding layer, every one of them a moving target that can break an install. Konnect is a single static binary — 20–25 MB depending on platform, a ~9 MB download. There is nothing to install alongside it and nothing to version-match.
SWIG is a dead end. The original's PCB backend depends on KiCAD's SWIG Python bindings, which KiCAD is deprecating in favor of its IPC API. SWIG also carried real operational scars: a zone-fill call that can segfault the backend, proxy-object comparison bugs, and a fallback path that can silently swap backends mid-session. Konnect talks to KiCAD 10 through the official IPC API (protobuf over NNG) — the interface KiCAD is investing in — with real-time board edits that integrate with KiCAD's own undo/redo.
Schematic edits should not corrupt files. Konnect edits .kicad_sch files
through its own S-expression engine with atomic writes (write, fsync, rename), UUID
preservation, and round-trip tests — no third-party schematic library with known
gaps, no text-manipulation workarounds.
Context economy is a feature. Exposing all 228 tools to an LLM costs roughly 23K
tokens of context on every listing. Konnect's router loads a starter kit (~2K
tokens) and lets the model pull in toolsets on demand — plus built-in observability
(get_recent_calls, server_stats, JSONL call logs) so the model can diagnose its
own tool failures.
The result is smaller, faster to install, aligned with where KiCAD is going, and built for production use rather than experimentation. The original project remains open, maintained, and useful — see the comparison below.
Instead of describing changes and applying them by hand, the AI works your project directly:
- Place and wire schematic components — add resistors, ICs, connectors; wire them together by pin name
- Lay out the PCB — place, move, rotate, and route footprints in real time via KiCAD's IPC API, with full undo/redo integration
- Run design checks — ERC, DRC, connectivity validation, decoupling audits, power-rail review, BOM health checks
- Export production files — Gerbers, drill, BOM, pick-and-place, 3D models, PDF
- Search JLCPCB parts — find in-stock components in a local 2.5M-part catalog and suggest alternatives
- Start from reference circuits — USB-C, LDO, buck converter, STM32, I2C, LED templates with verified component values
- Watch it happen — a live schematic viewer auto-refreshes as the AI edits
The full tool catalog is documented in tool-directory.md.
Explore the request path and safety boundaries in the interactive architecture diagrams. They are published from a standalone documentation repository and add no dependencies to Konnect.
- Download the package for your OS from Releases:
konnect-pcm-v<version>-windows.zip, -macos.zip, or -linux.zip. Each
bundles that platform's server binary — the macOS package is a universal
build, so one download covers Apple Silicon and Intel. (The konnect-pcm-* assets are the KiCAD plugin packages; the other archives are standalone
server binaries.)
- Open KiCAD 10 → Plugin and Content Manager
- Click Install from File and select the zip
- Restart KiCAD
Verify: open the PCB Editor → Tools → External Plugins → you should see Konnect.
For KiCad 10, the Konnect settings dialog also offers an optional native
Specctra bridge. When enabled, export_specctra_dsn can ask the active PCB
Editor to generate its native DSN while Konnect still binds the export to the
exact IPC snapshot and creates the strict reverse manifest used during SES
import. The bridge is local-only, authenticated, disabled by default, and not
the KiCad 11 integration path. Konnect uses its Rust exporter by default;
native_bridge_mode: "prefer" enables fallback to Rust when the bridge is
unavailable, while "require" refuses instead.
For end-to-end autorouting, run check_freerouting, then
export_specctra_dsn → route_specctra_dsn →
plan_specctra_ses_import / apply_specctra_ses. Readiness reports engine
discovery, native-MCP compatibility, and complete bridge availability
separately. The owned Java child is loopback-only and is reaped on success,
failure, timeout, or cancellation. The first supported profile preserves fixed
straight tracks and through vias; unlocked routing, arcs, zones, and unsupported
geometry are rejected before mutation.
# protoc is required (protobuf code generation), and cmake (the nng crate
# compiles the NNG C library with it).
# Windows: choco install protoc cmake
# macOS:   brew install protobuf cmake
# Linux:   apt install protobuf-compiler cmake
cargo build --release -p konnect
Konnect bundles shared KiCad skills for Claude and Codex. Select the client when installing, checking, or removing that guidance:
# Existing behavior remains the default: Claude skills, agents, and hooks
konnect init
# Codex installs only the shared skills under ~/.agents/skills
konnect init --client codex
konnect status --client codex
konnect uninstall --client codex
MCP server startup never installs or restores guidance. Run konnect init
explicitly when you want those files installed; after konnect uninstall,
starting the server leaves them removed.
Guidance written by an older konnect init is not updated by upgrading the
binary. konnect status compares every installed skill, agent, and hook with
the bundle in the binary you run and marks each current, different, or
missing. The server makes the same check once for each installed version:
the first start after konnect init compares the files, records
the result in ~/.konnect, and adds a one-line notice to its initialize
instructions if guidance is out of sync. Later starts reuse that record, so

ai_industry.title: Xiaomi Mijia Robot Vacuum 7 Max Launches With Advanced AI
ai_industry.summary_original: Xiaomi has officially introduced its newest robotic vacuum and mop system in China, the Mijia Robot Vacuum and Mop 7 Max. Serving as the successor to the Robot Vacuum 6 Max, this advanced home cleaning device is available in two distinct configurations: a sta…
ai_industry.content_original:
Xiaomi has officially introduced its newest robotic vacuum and mop system in China, the Mijia Robot Vacuum and Mop 7 Max. Serving as the successor to the Robot Vacuum 6 Max, this advanced home cleaning device is available in two distinct configurations: a standard version equipped with a water tank and an ultra-thin variant featuring a direct upper and lower water supply system.
The new model delivers a significant upgrade in raw performance, achieving a maximum negative pressure suction power of 45,000 Pa, compared to the 35,000 Pa offered by its predecessor. Additionally, the device intelligently detects specific functional areas such as kitchens or bathrooms, automatically spraying water heated to 50°C to tackle stubborn messes.
According to the manufacturer, the device achieves a floor sanitization rate of 99.99 percent. It features sophisticated recognition capabilities capable of identifying more than 320 distinct objects and types of debris, dynamically adjusting its cleaning pattern to prevent cable tangles.
Mechanical efficiency is further enhanced by three robotic arms designed to thoroughly clean room corners, walls, and furniture bases, with one arm specifically reaching edges outside the main roller’s range. The vacuum maintains a maximum obstacle-crossing height of 6 centimeters, matching the clearance capability of the previous generation. An integrated 3D area radar allows the chassis to seamlessly navigate under low clearance furniture like beds and cabinets while actively scraping debris and refreshing its cleaning mop.
Pricing and Availability
Pricing and availability details have been announced exclusively for the Chinese domestic market, with no official global release timeline provided yet. During the initial reservation period, the water tank version is priced at 4,999 Yuans (approximately $747 USD), while the ultra-thin variant carries a suggested retail price of 5,299 Yuans (approximately $792 USD).

ai_industry.title: The Fitbit Air Is Getting an Upgrade
ai_industry.summary_original: These are all the new features you can expect to see with the Air.
ai_industry.content_original:
Google is all about freshness for fall. In addition to announcing the new Fitbit Edge on Monday, the company also has three new features coming to its Fitbit Air, first released in May.
1. Health Guardian
There’s Health Guardian, Google’s proactive health and safety tools, available in the Google Health app. It works in the background to monitor your body’s health and wellness signals, provides a monthly summary of your health indicators and trends and sends timely notifications for anything that requires your immediate attention.
Health Guardian features
In the free Google Health app, Health Guardian includes irregular heart rhythm notifications and high and low heart rate notifications. With the Pixel Watch 3 and up, you also get loss-of-pulse notifications.
In the Premium version, which costs $10 monthly or $100 yearly, you can access these newer features: insulin resistance levels, blood pressure trends and sleep breathing quality trends. They work with the Pixel Watch 3 and up and the Fitbit Air.
Health Guardian will also come to the new Fitbit Edge, though we don’t have a specific date yet.
Insulin resistance
Insulin resistance refers to when your body doesn’t respond to insulin the way it should. Produced by your pancreas, insulin regulates your body’s glucose levels, moving glucose from your blood into your cells so that it can be used for energy.
Google Health’s insulin resistance doesn’t rely on readings from a continuous glucose monitor or lab work. Instead, it uses sensors on the Pixel Watch 3 and up and Fitbit Air to estimate insulin resistance and monitor shifts in your metabolic health.
Specifically, heart rhythm, sleep quality and daily activity data are tracked to give a user an idea of how efficiently their body absorbs energy from food and manages that energy during their activities.
Note that insulin resistance isn’t intended to monitor real-time glucose levels, and it isn’t a prescreener for diabetes or diabetes management.
Blood pressure
Blood pressure trends rely on optical and movement sensors, pulse and motion patterns and WavesFM, Google’s own AI foundation model, to measure your pulse’s shape and speed beneath your skin. This lets it estimate blood pressure over a month and give you a summary of your heart patterns.
However, blood pressure trends aren’t a replacement for a blood pressure monitor, so they shouldn’t be used for blood pressure management or as a prescreener for hypertension. It also isn’t designed for pregnant people.
Sleep breathing quality
For users aged 18 and up, sleep breathing quality tracks your breathing overnight to estimate how consistent and easy your breathing was during sleep. It uses your blood oxygen levels and your device’s heart rate and motion sensors.
With sleep breathing quality, you’ll see each morning how much of your sleep was spent in optimal breathing. Then, at the end of the month, you’ll receive an assessment showing those trends.
Remember that none of these features are for diagnosing or treating diseases.
2. Upgraded auto-activity detection
The Fitbit Air’s automatic workout detection has been upgraded to be twice as accurate, with 50% fewer missed detections when compared to the existing version. Its large language model can now better detect your workout type based on movement, your routine, logs and location.
For instance, it can better detect tennis and other racket sports, trail runs and HIIT.
When she reviewed the Fitbit Air, one of CNET Principal Writer Vanessa Hand Orellana’s biggest and only criticisms of the device was that it missed low-impact workouts like Pilates, so it’s great to see that the Fitbit team paid attention to consumer feedback when revamping its workout detection.
3. Metal mesh bands
With the Fitbit Air, you could previously choose either recycled polyester and elastane yarn bands or polyurethane bands. Now, metal mesh bands are available in silver and gold.
This makes the Air look more like jewelry and less like a fitness device. Perfect for those who prefer more discreet wearables that they can wear in any setting.

ai_industry.content_original:
37 tok/s from Qwen3-Next-80B (a 48 GB model) on a laptop with 32 GB of memory, 24 without drafts, where llama.cpp manages 2.8; reading a prompt, 62 tok/s against 16. Janas-LLM was faster than llama.cpp on every model compared on the same laptop (Debian 13 Linux, Intel Core Ultra 9 185H, its integrated Arc GPU, 32 GB, an NVMe SSD; 9-12 October 2026; the whole machine below):
The same models from other hands, in the catalog beside them:
Qwen3.8-27B: llama.cpp measured on 12 October 2026 (llama-bench -r 2), Janas-LLM on 13 October (janas-bench --prompt 1024 --gen 16, two rounds), once its prompt went whole to the GPU in one submission: 30.6 tok/s, where it read 26.4 the day before and 18.7 before the GPU's tiles for the IQ4_XS, IQ3_S and IQ4_NL weights of unsloth's UD mix. One exception: the 3-bit Qwen3-30B reads a prompt slower than llama.cpp, since its Q3_K weights do not go to the GPU's fast prompt yet; it writes three times as fast.
How they were measured, and the speeds with the drafts: What works now. On another machine the figures will be other ones: janas-bench measures yours.
Try it on Linux x86-64 (Ubuntu 22.04, Debian 12 and later):
curl -LO https://github.com/prabanta-dev/janas/releases/latest/download/janas-linux-x86_64.tar.gz
tar xf janas-linux-x86_64.tar.gz && cd janas
./janas-chat                     # the models it knows: pick one, it is downloaded and checked
Or on Windows 10 (1903 or later) and 11, x86-64: download janas-windows-x86_64.zip, unpack it, and in a terminal in its janas folder run .\janas-chat. On the same laptop under Windows 11 (12 October 2026) Janas-LLM wrote as fast as on Linux (Qwen3-4B 25.6 tok/s, Qwen3-30B-A3B 34.2) and read a prompt as fast with the mixture (Qwen3-30B-A3B 132 tok/s) and 1.8 times as fast with the dense model (Qwen3-4B 346 tok/s against 193), whose whole blocks go to the GPU, through Intel's own Windows driver there.
The models come already converted from Hugging Face; building from the sources: Getting started.

Janas is a family of tools for artificial intelligence, written in C with no dependencies beyond the C library. Its first component, Janas-LLM, runs large mixture-of-experts language models on ordinary computers, with or without a GPU: the weights stay on disk, the experts each token needs are streamed from an NVMe SSD, and the ones that keep coming back stay in memory. An 80-billion parameter model runs, and answers, on a laptop with 32 GB of RAM.
Designed and written by Maurizio "camauri" Cammalleri.
This is an experiment, not a product.
If something goes wrong, Ctrl-C stops a reply and Ctrl-D leaves the chat; --cache <GiB> puts a hard limit on the memory it takes, and JANAS_GPU=0 keeps it off the GPU entirely.
Everything in this repository was written and measured on:
- Linux Debian 13 (trixie), x86-64, kernel 6.12.107; GPU driver Mesa 26.1.6 (Vulkan); built with GCC 14.2
- Intel Core Ultra 9 185H (6 performance cores, 8 efficiency, 2 low-power; AVX2, FMA, F16C, AVX-VNNI; integrated Arc GPU)
- 32 GB of DDR5 RAM
- 1 TB NVMe SSD (about 5.7 GB/s reading)
The Windows build was run on the same laptop under Windows 11 (build 26300), with Intel's own graphics driver: its tests pass there, and how fast it was is under Or on Windows, above.
Everything the engine does is chosen from what it measures, so another machine will make other choices — that part is meant to travel. What has never been tried is the rest: other CPUs (especially without AVX-VNNI, or AMD), discrete GPUs, slower disks, more or less memory. If you run it somewhere else, the report from janas-bench is the single most useful thing you can send back (see Helping it run on more hardware).
What Janas-LLM runs today, model by model and feature by feature: docs/features.md.
On the machine above, with nothing else running, janas-bench reports this (measured on 10 October 2026, with the fast prompt the engine uses by default since that day):
Every figure is the mean of three rounds, not a best round, of the configuration the engine itself chose for each kind of pass - the one a chat runs: a prompt of 256 tokens, then 64 written. Here the integrated GPU reads every prompt (the fast prompt, below), and the threads the engine settled on were the performance cores' 12 for a prompt and for a single token on nearly every model, all the usable cores (performance and efficiency, not the low-power ones) for a few tokens at once. On another machine the engine may settle on other threads: the first passes of each kind try every core, one thread per performance core and the performance cores' threads, keep the fastest, and later try the others now and then, so that a machine that warms up can change the verdict (on an i9-14900HX every thread replied at less than half the speed of the performance cores' 16). The rounds run in alternating order so that the machine warming up and the cache filling weigh on each setting alike. Expect a few per cent either way between runs, and rather less than these on a first run, while the cache is still filling. Without the GPU (JANAS_GPU=0) Qwen3-4B reads the same prompt at 85 tok/s and writes at 27.
The last column is a draft guessing the next tokens and the model checking them, which is the same text at a higher rate — the whole of it is explained under --mtp: the Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.6 models' and Qwen3-Next's own prediction block, Gemma 4's assistant (a small drafting model of its own). It is measured on a chat reply: an ordinary question in English ("explain how bread is made at home"), 64 tokens of the answer, sampled as the chat samples. What the draft is worth depends on the text: there the drafts survived 74-89% of the time on the Qwen models and Gemma's two larger ones, 63-72% on Gemma's E2B and E4B; on Italian prose Qwen3.5-2B kept about a third of them, and gained next to nothing. One round of 64 tokens is noisy here, a tenth either way between runs. Qwen3-30B-A3B has no such block, nor have the dense Qwen3; the dense Qwen3.5 have one in their original checkpoint, which hf2jns_mtp converts (MODELS.md).
This column was wrong until 26 September 2026, and higher: it measured the block continuing a paragraph that repeated itself, which a model copies and the block guesses almost every time - 107 tok/s for Qwen3.5-2B, 26 for Qwen3.5-9B. The MoE figures of the time (29 and 30) happened to be lower than today's; the ChangeLog has the details.
The comparison with llama.cpp at the top of this page was measured so: llama.cpp (build 2b18470 of 18 September 2026) with its Vulkan backend on the same integrated GPU, everything on it (llama-bench -p 1024 -n 16 -ngl 99 -t 12; the largest model otherwise, below), against janas-bench --prompt 1024 --gen 16 on the same files the same days (9-12 October 2026; llama.cpp's best configuration, Janas-LLM's own choice; on 11 October three rounds each, llama-bench -r 3 and janas-bench --rounds 3, for Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3.5-0.8B, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and the models from other hands; Qwen3-Coder-Next as Qwen3-Next-80B, below).

ai_industry.title: This unofficial port brings Pixel 11's Rambler to any Android phone
ai_industry.summary_original: A developer has found a way to bring the Pixel 11's exclusive Rambler AI voice typing feature to other Android phones.
ai_industry.content_original:
This unofficial port brings Pixel 11's Rambler to any Android phone
A developer has found a way to bring the Pixel 11's exclusive Rambler AI voice typing feature to other Android phones.
What you need to know
- Google's Rambler uses AI to clean up voice typing, removing filler words, correcting grammar, and formatting text.
- Developer Akshay Kadam has released PixelBoard, a modified Gboard APK that enables Rambler on other Android phones.
- Users can reportedly access Rambler by installing PixelBoard and setting it as their default keyboard instead of Gboard.
If you've ever wanted to try the Pixel 11's Rambler feature on your Android phone, you can now do so, although there's a catch.
The Google Pixel 11 series launched earlier this year with several new AI features, including Magic Cue, Magic Capture, and Rambler. For those unfamiliar, Rambler is Google's new AI-powered voice typing feature that offers a much more advanced experience than the regular voice typing we've had on Android phones for years.
Similar to AI voice typing tools that have been available on desktops for a while, Rambler automatically cleans up your speech, fixes grammar and formatting, and removes filler words like "um" and "uh" to give you properly formatted text. It can also understand corrections while you're speaking, add emojis, and even rewrite your text in different tones, such as formal or casual.
Unlike traditional voice typing, though, Rambler doesn't show a live transcription of everything you're saying. Instead, once you've finished speaking and tapped the Done button, it processes your speech and returns a cleaned-up, properly formatted version of what you said.
The feature has been exclusive to the Pixel 11 series so far, but a developer has now found a way to bring it to other Android devices.
Developer Akshay Kadam has shared a modified version of Google's Gboard app, called PixelBoard, on GitHub. The developer has patched the Gboard APK to enable Rambler on Android phones that don't officially support the feature.
According to the developer, you can install the modified APK on your Android device and switch your default keyboard from Gboard to PixelBoard to access Rambler without needing a Pixel 11.
Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android
That said, PixelBoard isn't an official Google app, and installing modified APK files always carries security and privacy risks. There's also no guarantee that Rambler will continue working through this method. Since the feature is officially exclusive to the Pixel 11 series, Google could block the workaround through a future Gboard or server-side update.
But if you're curious about Rambler, the developer's GitHub project offers an unofficial way to try the feature without buying a Pixel 11. Just keep in mind that you're installing a modified keyboard at your own risk.
